name: Transit supply: scheduled service by stop pattern, route and stop, hour by hour
plain: How much scheduled service each route, each direction of a route and each stop has, hour by hour, on a weekday, a Saturday and a Sunday. It is built from the published timetables, so it shows the service operators plan, not the service that ran.
definition: transit_supply.json has one section per day type (wk: a typical weekday; sa: Saturday; su: Sunday). Each section has four parts. patterns: one row per stop pattern (see Stop pattern), with the operator (o), route (r), mode (m), whether the operator's timetable is current (cur), number of stops, length along the route line in km, trips, trips per hour (hours, 24 values by the hour of the departure from the first stop), first and last departure in seconds after midnight, trips and average wait in four periods (periods: am 06:00-09:00, mid 09:00-15:00, pm 15:00-19:00, eve 19:00-23:00), median run time in minutes, scheduled speed in km/h, and whether the path follows the route line (line). routes: one row per operator and route label, adding up its patterns (both directions), with peak_hw, the average wait at the morning peak of its busiest pattern. stops: one row per stop id (the ids of transport.json) with departures (n), departures per hour (hours), the routes that depart from it, first and last departure and the longest wait between 06:00 and 22:00 (gap, minutes). island: for each hour, vehicles in service, routes running, stops with a departure and stops with frequent service (frequent_per_hour, 4: a departure every 15 minutes or better), counting only current timetables. In the 2026-10 snapshot, a weekday has 222 stop patterns, 144 routes and 2,866 stops with departures; 38 of the 144 routes run on an expired timetable.
geography: Each stop pattern, route and stop with a timetable

coverage.frequency: Recomputed every night with the transit refresh, and written only when a value changed (whether a timetable is current changes with the date).

method: supply.py reads trips.json, trips_sa.json and trips_su.json (format 2: each trip's stop pattern, where its stops are on the pattern's path and its stop times; trip_paths.py) and the feed status of each operator in operators.json. A trip counts in the hour of its departure from its first stop. A departure is every stop time of a trip except its last stop, where the vehicle arrives. The average wait in a period is the period's length divided by its trips (180 minutes and 6 trips give 30 minutes); it is not the longest wait. Run time is the median of the pattern's trips; the scheduled speed is its length along the route line over that time. A row is current (cur) when its operator's feed status is current or expiring on the day of the build.
how_to_read: Use the patterns to compare service by direction, the routes to compare routes, and the stops to see where and when people can board. Look at trips per hour and the wait at the peak together with the span (first and last departure): a route with a short wait but service only in the morning serves fewer trips in a day than its peak suggests. Compare current and expired timetables separately.
caveats: Timetables, not observed service: a trip may not run, run late or be added without the feed saying so.
Expired timetables (cur false) may still run, run differently, or not run at all.
Públicos are in no timetable, so they are not counted; where públicos run, the real service is higher.
About 8.9% of weekday stop calls have no time in the feeds and are not counted as departures.
The average wait is a planning figure for the whole period. Irregular timetables can have much longer single waits; the longest wait at each stop (gap) shows that.

name: Stop pattern (a variant of a route)
plain: The trips of a route that stop at the same places in the same order. A route usually has at least two, one for each direction, and more when some trips skip stops or end early.
definition: A stop pattern is the ordered list of stops of a trip. Trips with the same operator, route label and stops, in the same order, share one pattern. trip_paths.py stores each pattern once, as a path along the route line (paths), with its stop ids (path_stops); each trip names its pattern (k). In the 2026-10 snapshot, the 3,297 weekday trips share 222 patterns.

coverage.frequency: Rebuilt from the feeds every night when a feed changes.

method: trip_paths.py groups the trips of each day by operator, route label and the coordinates of their stops, in order.
how_to_read: Supply by pattern is supply in one direction. A route's total adds up its patterns, so it counts both directions.

view.label: 3D view, Route tab: Existing routes (one row per direction)

name: Trips per hour
plain: How many trips of a route or direction leave in each hour of the day, by the timetable.
definition: The number of trips whose departure from their first stop falls in the hour (07:00 to 07:59 counts as 07:00). For a stop, the same count uses the departures from that stop.
geography: Each stop pattern, route and stop with a timetable

coverage.frequency: Recomputed with the transit supply file.

method: supply.py, from the stop times in the trips files.
how_to_read: On the 3D view, Service at this hour draws routes and stops by this count for the hour on the clock: 1, 2-3, 4-5, and 6 or more per hour. Where several routes share a road, the lines overlap; the widest shows the busiest route, not their total.

view.label: 3D view, Time tab: Service at this hour

name: Average wait between departures (headway)
plain: How many minutes, on average, pass between one departure and the next in a part of the day: the morning peak (06:00-09:00), midday (09:00-15:00), the afternoon peak (15:00-19:00) and the evening (19:00-23:00).
definition: The length of the period in minutes divided by the trips of a stop pattern that leave in it. Blank when no trip leaves in the period. For a route, the morning peak wait is that of its busiest pattern (one direction).
geography: Each stop pattern and route with a timetable

coverage.frequency: Recomputed with the transit supply file.

method: supply.py: periods[name].hw = (minutes in the period) / (trips in the period), rounded.
how_to_read: Planners often treat 15 minutes or less as service people can use without a timetable. An average hides irregular timetables: a route with 4 trips in 3 hours averages 45 minutes even if two of them leave together.
caveats: An average over the period, not the longest wait; see Longest wait at a stop.

view.label: Route planner: Existing service near this route

name: Span of service (first and last departure)
plain: The time of the first and the last departure of the day for a route, a direction or a stop.
definition: The earliest and the latest departure from the first stop (for a pattern or route) or from the stop (for a stop), in seconds after midnight in the file and as hours and minutes on the page.
geography: Each stop pattern, route and stop with a timetable

coverage.frequency: Recomputed with the transit supply file.

method: supply.py: first and last of the sorted departure times.
how_to_read: A short span leaves out early workers and evening trips home even when the peak service is good.

name: Longest wait at a stop
plain: The longest time between two departures at a stop between 06:00 and 22:00, counting from 06:00 to the first departure and from the last departure to 22:00.
definition: The largest gap, in minutes, between consecutive departures at the stop (any route), with 06:00 and 22:00 as the edges of the window. Blank when the stop has no departure in the window.

coverage.frequency: Recomputed with the transit supply file.

how_to_read: A stop with many departures can still have a long gap in the middle of the day. In the 2026-10 snapshot, even the busiest weekday stops (254 departures) have a longest wait of 18 to 28 minutes.

view.label: 3D view: click a stop of Stops by departures in the hour

name: Frequent service (a departure every 15 minutes or better)
plain: A stop has frequent service in an hour when 4 or more departures leave from it in that hour, any route.
definition: frequent_per_hour in transit_supply.json (4). The island counts (island.frequent_stops) give, for each hour, the stops with a current timetable that reach it.

coverage.frequency: Recomputed with the transit supply file.

how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, about 280 stops have frequent service in each weekday hour from 07:00 to 18:00 (282 at 08:00), out of 2,261 stops with a departure in that hour. The access measures use another threshold (20 or more weekday departures in the day); say which one a figure uses.

name: Service at this hour (3D view, Time tab)
plain: Routes drawn by the trips they run in the hour on the clock, and stops sized by their departures in that hour, for a weekday, Saturday or Sunday, with a chart of vehicles in service through the day.
definition: Two switches and a summary in the Time tab of the 3D view. Routes by trips in the hour draws each stop pattern with trips in that hour along its path, by trips per hour (1, 2-3, 4-5, 6 or more). Stops by departures in the hour draws each stop with a departure in that hour, by its departures. The summary gives, for the hour, vehicles in service, routes running, stops with a departure and stops with frequent service; the chart gives vehicles in service for every hour (click a bar to move the clock). A click on a route or a stop of these layers opens its card, before the map's own features drawn under it: a stop of the Stops layer, a cluster of stops, a route line or an area. The day buttons (Weekday, Saturday, Sunday) choose the timetable for the replay and for these layers. Expired timetables are left out unless Include operators whose timetable has expired is checked.
method: supply3d.js reads transit_supply.json and the paths of the day's trips file; the layers change when the hour on the clock changes.
how_to_read: Play the day to see where service starts, peaks and stops. Places with no line or dot in an hour have no scheduled service then. Click a route for its trips in the hour and a link to its profile; click a stop for its departures, routes and longest wait.
caveats: Where several routes share a road, the lines overlap; the widest shows the busiest route, not their total.

view.label: 3D view, Time tab: Service at this hour

name: Route profile (3D view, Route tab)
plain: Choose an existing route to see its service hour by hour, the wait between departures in each direction, its stops and the routes of any operator that stop within 250 m of it. The route is highlighted on the map, with its stops and the stops of the connecting routes.
definition: The Existing routes section of the Route tab. The card shows the route's operator and mode, whether its timetable is current (with the feed's end date), trips on a weekday, Saturday and Sunday, first and last departure, the morning-peak wait of its busiest direction, departures by hour, a table of its directions (stop patterns) with trips, the average wait in four periods, run time, length and scheduled speed, the stops of its busiest direction with each stop's departures (all routes) and longest wait, and its connections: routes with a weekday departure from a stop within 250 m of one of its stops, other operators first.
method: supply3d.js, from transit_supply.json, the trips files (paths and path_stops), transport.json (stop names and positions) and operators.json (feed dates). Connections are found on a grid of the stops with weekday departures, by straight-line distance.
how_to_read: Connections are places where two routes can meet, by distance only: the card does not yet check whether their times fit (a short wait to change). Phase 3 of the transit analysis plan adds that.
caveats: 250 m in a straight line, not a walking route.

name: Existing service near a planned route
plain: For a route drawn in the route planner: the stops with a current timetable within 400 m of it, their departures between 7:00 and 8:00 on a weekday, the share of the route with no such stop within 400 m, and the routes that stop near it.
definition: Stops with a current timetable (transit_supply.json, weekday) within 400 m in a straight line of the planned route; departures from them in the 07:00 hour; the share of points every 100 to 500 m along the route (depending on its length) with no such stop within 400 m; and the routes departing from those stops with their weekday trips and morning-peak wait. The residents count beside it (residents with no stop with a current timetable within 400 m) uses the same current stops.
geography: A route drawn by the user

coverage.frequency: Calculated in your browser each time a route is planned

method: plan.js (score), on a grid of about 500 m of the current stops.
how_to_read: A planned route that runs along existing frequent service adds little; one with a high share far from any current stop, and many residents near it, points to a gap. A planning aid, not a demand forecast.
caveats: Before this measure, the residents count treated stops with an expired timetable as service; it now counts only current timetables when the supply file loads.
